hints: Think about what makes benzene especially stable compared to an ordinary alkene, focusing on its ring of pi electrons.
walkthrough:
Picture what addition would do to benzene**
Imagine $\text{Br}_2$ adding across one of the double bonds like it does with ethene. You would break the continuous ring of p orbitals. The product would be a non-aromatic diene with localised double bonds.

See why substitution wins**
In substitution, $\text{Br}$ replaces $\text{H}$ but the flat ring with 6 delocalised pi-electrons is reformed at the end. Keeping that aromatic stabilisation is energetically far more favourable, so no addition takes place.
Final answer: Substitution retains the aromatic ring stabilised by delocalisation of 6 pi-electrons, whereas addition would destroy the delocalised system and its stability.

hints: Start from the electron rich benzene pi cloud attacking the strong electrophile $\text{Br}^+$.
Recall that attack by one carbon breaks aromaticity temporarily to give a positively charged cyclohexadienyl intermediate.
Think how aromaticity can be restored by removing the proton from the same carbon that gained $\text{Br}$.
walkthrough:
Make the first bond with the electrophile**
Benzene is electron rich. Draw a curly arrow starting in the middle of the benzene ring, representing a pair of pi-electrons, pointing to the $\text{Br}^+$ ion. This forms a new $\text{C-Br}$ bond at one carbon.

Draw the Wheland intermediate correctly**
That carbon now has both $\text{Br}$ and $\text{H}$ and becomes tetrahedral, $\text{sp}^3$. The positive charge is left delocalised over the remaining five carbons of the ring. Show this with a circle broken at that carbon plus delocalised + charge, or with three resonance forms.

Restore aromaticity by losing a proton**
Draw a second curly arrow from the $\text{C-H}$ bond on that same tetrahedral carbon back into the ring. The $\text{H}$ leaves as $\text{H}^+$, the pi system closes back to 6 electrons, and bromobenzene, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Br}$, is formed.

Final answer: Curly arrow from benzene pi-system to $\text{Br}^+$ to form Wheland arenium intermediate with $\text{Br}$ and $\text{H}$ on same tetrahedral carbon and positive charge delocalised in ring. Curly arrow from C-H bond to reform aromatic ring, losing $\text{H}^+$ to give bromobenzene, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Br} + \text{H}^+$.

hints: Remember the $\text{H}^+$ lost in (a)(ii) must react with the $\text{AlBr}_4^-$ formed when $\text{AlBr}_3 + \text{Br}_2$ made $\text{Br}^+$.
walkthrough:
Balance the catalyst cycle**
When $\text{AlBr}_3$ polarised $\text{Br}_2$, it became $\text{AlBr}_4^-$. That ion is a base for the $\text{H}^+$ expelled from the Wheland intermediate. Joining them gives $\text{HBr}$ and frees $\text{AlBr}_3$ again: $$\text{AlBr}_4^- + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{AlBr}_3 + \text{HBr}$$ This shows $\text{AlBr}_3$ is unchanged overall, as a true catalyst.

hints: Compare the $\text{-OH}$ group in phenol with $\text{-H}$ in benzene, focusing on the lone pairs on oxygen.
Link increased electron density in the ring to easier attack on a non-polar $\text{Br}_2$ molecule without a catalyst.
walkthrough:
See how OH pumps electrons into the ring**
In phenol, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}$, one lone pair on oxygen overlaps with the ring pi system and is delocalised into it. That pushes extra negative charge into the ring, especially at the 2, 4 and 6 positions.

Link electron richness to reactivity**
A more electron rich ring is a stronger nucleophile. It is able to distort the electron cloud of a neutral $\text{Br}_2$ molecule and induce the $\delta+$ end needed for attack. Benzene is less electron rich and needs $\text{AlBr}_3$ to generate the much stronger electrophile $\text{Br}^+$, but phenol reacts readily with $\text{Br}_2$ alone.

Final answer: Lone pair on oxygen in phenol is delocalised into the benzene ring. This increases electron density in the ring so phenol can polarise / induce a dipole in $\text{Br}_2$, so no $\text{AlBr}_3$ catalyst is needed.

hints: Count carbons: you need all distinct skeletons with formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9^+$ starting from the given primary straight chain $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2^+$.
Think of the branched $\text{C}_4$ skeleton with a three carbon chain plus a methyl branch, and place $+$ on different carbons.
Remember the highly branched skeleton with a central carbon joined to three methyl groups gives the tertiary ion.
walkthrough:
Keep the straight chain but move the charge**
Structure 1 is the primary n-butyl cation, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2^+$. Keeping the same four carbon chain, moving $+$ to carbon 2 gives the secondary ion $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}^+\text{CH}_3$.

Branch the chain**
Rearrange to a $\text{C}_3$ chain with a methyl branch: $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{CH-}$. Putting $\text{CH}_2^+$ at the end gives the primary branched ion $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{CHCH}_2^+$.

Make the tertiary ion**
Put the positive carbon in the centre joined to three $\text{CH}_3$ groups to get $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{C}^+$, the tert-butyl cation. These are the three other distinct $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9^+$ isomers.
Final answer: Structure 2: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}^+\text{CH}_3$; Structure 3: $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{CHCH}_2^+$; Structure 4: $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{C}^+$ in any order.

hints: Each carbocation attaches through its $\text{C}^+$ carbon to benzene to give a $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{14}$ butylbenzene isomer.
Use symmetry: a tert-butyl group has three equivalent methyl carbons, greatly reducing the number of $^{13}\text{C}$ peaks.
Count distinct carbons: monosubstituted benzene always gives 4 ring signals, plus the number of distinct alkyl carbons.
Match the most symmetric product to 6 peaks, the isobutyl product to 7 peaks, and the sec-butyl product to 8 peaks.
walkthrough:
Build the four alkylation products**
Benzene + $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2^+$ gives n-butylbenzene, already drawn. Benzene + $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{C}^+$ gives $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{C(CH}_3\text{)}_3$. Benzene + $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{CHCH}_2^+$ gives $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)}_2$. Benzene + $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}^+\text{CH}_3$ gives $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$.

Apply carbon-13 NMR equivalence**
A monosubstituted benzene ring alone shows 4 peaks. Then add alkyl carbons. For $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{C(CH}_3\text{)}_3$, the three methyl carbons are identical, so 4 + 1 quaternary + 1 methyl type = 6 peaks. This must be the 6-peak spectrum.

Distinguish 7 peaks from 8 peaks**
For $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)}_2$, the two methyls are equivalent: 4 ring + $\text{CH}_2$ + $\text{CH}$ + 1 methyl type = 7 peaks. For $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, all four alkyl carbons are different: 4 ring + 4 alkyl = 8 peaks, same count as n-butylbenzene but a different isomer.

Assign the structures**
So link 6 peaks to tert-butylbenzene, 7 peaks to isobutylbenzene (2-methyl-1-phenylpropane), and the second 8-peak spectrum to sec-butylbenzene (2-phenylbutane). Symmetry is the key tool for choosing between them.

Final answer: 6 peaks: tert-butylbenzene, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{C(CH}_3\text{)}_3$; 7 peaks: 2-methyl-1-phenylpropane, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)}_2$; 8 peaks: 2-phenylbutane, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. Given 8-peak compound is n-butylbenzene, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$.
